content: Physical activity is essential for children and adolescents, and it is never too late to start. If you are not currently active, begin with small steps and gradually increase your activity level until you meet the recommended guidelines. Every form of physical activity counts, whether it is part of work, sports, leisure, transportation, or household tasks. Engage in activities daily in ways that suit you best. Muscle-strengthening exercises are beneficial for everyone, and older adults should incorporate activities that focus on balance and coordination to prevent falls and improve overall health. Excessive sedentary behavior can be harmful to health. Even low-intensity activities are better than remaining still. Everyone can benefit from moving more. Physical activity can be categorized into different intensities: Low-intensity aerobic activity: Activities such as slow walking, washing dishes, or playing a musical instrument allow you to talk or sing comfortably. Moderate-intensity aerobic activity: Activities like brisk walking, jogging, cycling leisurely, or playing sports such as badminton or tennis allow you to carry on a conversation. High-intensity aerobic activity: Activities such as hiking, fast cycling, swimming, or playing basketball make talking difficult due to the intensity. Bone-strengthening activities: Weight-bearing activities like walking, hiking, traditional dancing, or yoga help strengthen bones. Muscle-strengthening activities: Exercises like resistance training, push-ups, pull-ups, or carrying heavy loads engage all major muscle groups. Stretching: Intentional stretching improves muscle elasticity and flexibility. For children under 5 years old: Infants under 1 year should have at least 30 minutes of floor-based play (e.g., tummy time) daily and should not be restrained in swings or car seats for more than an hour. Children aged 1–2 years should engage in at least 180 minutes of active play spread throughout the day. Children aged 3–4 years should also have at least 180 minutes of active play, with at least 60 minutes being moderate to vigorous activity. For children and adolescents aged 5–17 years: They should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily, primarily aerobic in nature. For adults aged 18–64 years: At least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 15 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity should be performed at least five days per week. Adults with chronic diseases or disabilities may need to consult healthcare professionals for tailored advice. For pregnant and postpartum women: Regular physical activity provides benefits such as reduced risks of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and postpartum depression. At least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity five days per week is recommended. Pelvic floor exercises are particularly beneficial for maintaining muscle tone and aiding recovery after delivery. For older adults aged 65 and above: At least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 15 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity should be performed at least five days per week. Additionally, multi-component activities focusing on balance and strength should be included at least three days per week to prevent falls and maintain functional abilities. Safety considerations are crucial when engaging in physical activity: Start slowly and gradually increase the intensity and duration of activities. Warm up before and cool down after exercise. Wear appropriate clothing and footwear, and stay hydrated. Avoid outdoor activities during peak sun hours and ensure a safe environment for exercise. Individuals with chronic conditions or disabilities should consult healthcare professionals for personalized recommendations. Pre-exercise medical clearance is generally unnecessary for lightto moderate-intensity activities unless contraindications exist.
